S1.title: Calderbrook Borough Council: Permits Online
S1.facts:
Calderbrook Borough Council is a mid-sized council in the English Midlands serving about 180,000 residents. Each year its parking services team issues around 26,000 resident permits, visitor vouchers and business permits. Almost every application arrives on paper or by email and is keyed in by hand by a team of nine permit officers. Processing takes an average of 11 working days. Residents complain about lost forms, queues at the town hall customer centre and having to post copies of their council tax bill and vehicle documents. Last year 31% of calls to the council's contact centre were about permits.

The council's five-year corporate plan commits it to services that are digital by preference, a 20% cut in the cost of transactional services and net zero council operations by 2035. In January the chief executive's office issued a mandate for a project to replace the paper process with an online permit service that residents can use on a phone, with automatic checks against council tax and vehicle records and a smaller team handling the exceptions. The current permit database runs on software whose support contract ends on 31 October next year. Extending support would cost £140,000 for one more year, and the finance team has said that money is not available.

Calderbrook has run few projects of this size. Its project management office of two people keeps a portfolio list and some templates, but there is no consistent method. A recent waste collection app went 40% over budget and was launched without the contact centre being told, which led to a week of complaints. The council has decided to use PRINCE2 7 on Permits Online and to treat the project as a pilot for wider use of the method.

The council has no in-house developers. After a mini-competition on a public sector framework it appointed Kestrel Lane Digital, a 60-person agency that builds public services using Scrum in two-week sprints, under a time-and-materials contract capped at £620,000. The council intends to act as a thin client: Kestrel Lane will design, build and host the service, and the council will own the product, set priorities and run the service once it is live. Integration with the council tax system needs work from the council's own ICT team of four, which is also supporting three other projects this year.

The approved budget is £780,000, covering the supplier cap, council staff time and a contingency. The leadership team has said it will accept some risk to the speed of delivery, but it has a very low appetite for risks to residents' personal data and to accessibility. The service must meet the WCAG 2.2 AA standard, pass an independent accessibility audit and pass an IT health check before it goes live. The council's digital service standard also requires every new service to be tested with real users, including people who use assistive technology.

The expected benefits are a cut in processing time from 11 days to 2, contact centre permit calls halved within a year of launch, a reduction of five posts in parking services through natural turnover rather than redundancy, and about 1.2 tonnes less paper a year. The trade union has asked for assurances about the staff affected and wants to be consulted on the new ways of working. Several ward councillors are worried that older residents without internet access will be left behind. The Old Town Residents' Association, in the ward with the highest permit demand, has asked to take part in testing.

The project will start with a six-week initiation stage. Kestrel Lane will then run a discovery and alpha stage to understand users and test prototypes, followed by a private beta stage in the Old Town ward only, in which real permits are issued online alongside the paper route. The final stage is a public beta for the whole borough, the migration of all existing permits from the old database and the closure of the paper process. A telephone assisted route will remain for residents who cannot apply online. The chief executive's office expects the board to consider at the end of each stage whether the project is still worth continuing.

S2.title: Tarnside College: Engineering Skills Centre
S2.facts:
Tarnside College is a further education college on the north-east coast of England with 7,500 students. It has secured a £4.2 million capital grant from the regional combined authority's skills fund to convert a vacant 2,400 square metre warehouse next to its main campus into an Engineering Skills Centre. The centre will train 300 apprentices a year in welding, electrical installation and wind turbine maintenance. Two offshore wind operators and several local manufacturers have pledged apprentice places, on condition that the centre opens for the September intake in 20 months' time.

The total project budget is £5.1 million: the grant plus £0.9 million from college reserves. The grant must be claimed in full by 31 March of the second year, in quarterly claims supported by evidence of spend. Any overspend falls on the college, and the grant can be clawed back if the centre is not delivering apprenticeships within six months of the end of the grant period. The college's board of governors has told the principal that the September opening date cannot move and that the college cannot afford to spend more than 3% above the approved budget.

The work will be delivered in a linear-sequential way. An external architect will complete the design, and the college will then tender a design-and-build contract. A survey has found asbestos-containing materials that must be removed before structural work starts. The structural works include a new mezzanine floor. Mechanical and electrical fit-out follows, then the installation of specialist equipment: 24 welding bays with fume extraction and a wind turbine nacelle training rig made by a manufacturer in Denmark, which has a 30-week lead time from order. The college also needs new apprenticeship courses designed and approved, and eight instructors recruited, so that teaching can start on the opening day. The college's curriculum team will do this work alongside the building works.

The college declared a climate emergency two years ago. Its targets for this project are embodied carbon of no more than 350 kgCO2e per square metre for the refurbishment, 90% of construction waste diverted from landfill, and a building heated by air-source heat pumps with solar panels on the roof. The combined authority scores grant compliance partly against these targets. The cost consultant's pre-tender estimate is already £4.95 million before contingency, and the heat pumps are the largest single cost after the structural works.

Safety is a major concern. The warehouse is next to the student entrance, and about 1,800 students aged 16 to 18 use the main campus every day. Site traffic must not cross the pedestrian route. The college's last building project, a small science lab refurbishment, had a reportable incident when a contractor's van reversed into a member of staff. One governor has said she wants safety to be reported to the board at every meeting.

The college estates department has delivered small refurbishments but nothing of this scale. The college will act as a relatively thick client: it will appoint its own project manager on a fixed-term contract, retain an external cost consultant and keep the head of estates closely involved, while the main contractor manages the works on site. The vice principal for curriculum has asked for 30 welding bays rather than 24, and the wind operators have said the nacelle rig is the main reason they are committing apprentices. The finance and resources committee of the governors meets every two months and has asked to be told immediately of any forecast overspend.

The college has used PRINCE2 7 on two smaller projects. The lessons report from the lab refurbishment said that contractor progress was reported only verbally, that changes were agreed on site without anyone checking the budget, and that the curriculum team was not involved until a month before handover.

S3.title: Wenmoor Community Health: Single Point of Access
S3.facts:
Wenmoor Community Health is a publicly funded provider of community health services in the north of England. It employs 2,300 staff and provides district nursing, community therapy and rehabilitation to about 420,000 people across three localities: Eastfield (urban), Moorside (rural) and Holtby (coastal). Referrals from GPs, hospitals and social care reach the service through 14 different routes, including email inboxes, phone lines and, at two sites, fax machines. The average time from referral to first contact is nine days. Last year 6% of referrals were lost or duplicated, and a serious incident review found that a housebound patient with a pressure ulcer had waited three weeks because her referral was sent to the wrong locality.

The local commissioner has made a single point of access (SPA) a condition of next year's contract. The SPA will provide one phone number and one electronic referral route for all three localities, a clinical triage hub staffed by senior nurses and therapists on rotation, standard triage criteria, and new rotas. The patient record system already has a referral module that has never been switched on. It will be configured by the system's supplier under the existing support contract, so no new software needs to be bought.

Wenmoor's project management office was disbanded in a restructure two years ago. Since then, most change has been led by clinicians alongside their day jobs. Staff turnover is 17% and a recent staff survey showed low morale. Many district nurses fear that a central triage hub will take away their professional judgement about which patients they see first. A previous attempt to introduce central booking in Moorside was abandoned after four months in 2021, and nobody recorded why. The trust board has asked for PRINCE2 7 to be used and for a written record of what is learned.

The project will design the SPA with staff and patients, run a pilot in Eastfield, evaluate it and then roll out to Moorside and Holtby. The budget is £650,000, mostly to backfill clinical time and pay for training, funded from the commissioner's transformation money. The commissioner expects the SPA to be live in all three localities within 18 months and will withhold part of the contract value if it is not.

The expected benefits are referral to first contact cut from nine days to three, lost or duplicated referrals below 0.5%, and 20% fewer unnecessary home visits, which would free capacity for patients with complex needs. Staff travel mileage is expected to fall by 15%, supporting the trust's net zero plan. One expected dis-benefit is that district nursing teams will no longer control which referrals they accept.

The trust has a low appetite for any risk to clinical safety. Any change to triage criteria must be signed off by the trust's clinical safety officer and the medical director before it is used. The appetite for risk to administrative processes is moderate. Patient data may only be shared through approved systems.

Most project team members work part-time or on rotas across the three localities and can usually only join meetings online at lunchtime. Several GP practices in Moorside have said they will keep faxing referrals to the nurses they know, and the chair of the Moorside GP federation has publicly questioned whether the SPA is needed in a rural area. The patients' forum supports the change but wants carers to be able to refer directly. The union representing nursing staff has asked to see the new rotas before they are agreed.

The trust's executive team will accept a cost variation of plus or minus 10% and a delay of up to one month to the end of the roll-out; anything beyond that must go to the trust board. The commissioning manager has asked to sit on the project board so that she can see progress at first hand, and the head of nursing for Eastfield has asked whether the triage hub could start in her locality before initiation is finished, because her team is already overstretched.

S4.title: Fernhollow Foods: Fernhollow Kitchen range launch
S4.facts:
Fernhollow Foods is a family-owned food manufacturer in Somerset with 320 staff. It makes chilled soups and sauces, almost all of them sold as own-label products for two supermarket chains. Sales have been flat for three years and margins are falling. The board has decided to build its own brand. In March the managing director issued a mandate for a project to launch Fernhollow Kitchen, a range of six plant-based chilled ready meals.

The sales and marketing director has secured a listing with Harbridge's, a national supermarket, for 400 stores from the first week of next February, eleven months away. Fernhollow has paid a listing fee of £180,000. If it misses the launch week, the slot is lost until the following year and the fee is not refunded. Harbridge's has said it will accept a launch of four recipes if six are not ready, but not fewer than four.

The delivery approach is a hybrid. Recipes, branding and packaging design will be developed iteratively: chefs and a design agency, Mint and Tallow, will work in two-week cycles with fortnightly tastings by a consumer panel. The factory work is linear. A new tray-sealing line must be bought from a Dutch equipment supplier, with a 14-week lead time and a three-week factory shutdown to install it. Two of the six recipes need a pan-frying process that Fernhollow does not have, so they will be made by a co-manufacturer, Greendale Ready Meals, under a supply agreement with minimum annual volumes. A packaging supplier will provide the trays and sleeves.

Each supplier has a different contract: Mint and Tallow is paid a fixed price per phase; the line supplier has a fixed-price contract with penalties for late delivery; Greendale requires Fernhollow to buy at least 150,000 meals in the first year. The finance director is worried about this minimum volume if sales are slow.

The approved budget is £2.3 million. The board has said the launch week cannot move. Every recipe must have a shelf life of at least eight days, meet Harbridge's technical standard and pass its audit, and be made under allergen controls. One recipe uses sesame, which has never been handled on the Fernhollow site. The board wants all packaging to be recyclable at the kerbside and a carbon label on every pack, with a footprint of no more than 1.5 kg CO2e per meal.

The business case forecasts branded sales of £6 million a year by year three and a gross margin of 28%. The board is willing to take commercial risk to build the brand, but has a very low appetite for food safety and allergen risks: a product recall would put the own-label contracts, which provide 85% of revenue, at risk.

Fernhollow's directors are used to running the factory, not projects. The new project manager joined from a larger food company where she used PRINCE2. The sales and marketing director has already told the Harbridge's buyer that all six recipes will launch. The operations director wants the line installation to happen after the Christmas peak, which would leave five weeks for factory trials before launch. The head of new product development says the chefs need at least four more consumer panel rounds before the recipes are final.

The project plan has five stages. Initiation will take four weeks. A concept and recipe stage will choose the final recipes and brand. A development stage will finalize recipes, packaging and the co-manufacturing agreement while the line is built and installed. A trials stage will run factory trials, shelf-life tests and the supermarket audit. The final stage covers launch and the first eight weeks of sales, after which the range will be handed to the normal sales and operations teams.

S5.title: Carrowford City Council: Carrowford Half Marathon and Festival
S5.facts:
Carrowford is a city of about 300,000 people. Its city council has adopted an Active Carrowford strategy to raise physical activity levels and to promote the city as a visitor destination. As part of the strategy, the council's director of culture, leisure and tourism has been given a mandate to deliver the first Carrowford Half Marathon and riverside festival weekend on Sunday 14 September next year. The date has been agreed with the national athletics body and the road closures have been booked; it cannot move.

The target is 8,000 runners and 25,000 spectators. The council expects the event to bring about £2.5 million into local businesses over the weekend, with 30% of entrants living in the city and 40% running their first half marathon. Partner charities hope to raise £400,000. The council plans to repeat the event every year if the first one succeeds, run by its events team as part of normal business.

The council's events team has run many small events, such as markets and park concerts, but nothing of this scale. It has contracted Paceline Events, a specialist race management company, to provide the course design, timing, race-day operations and medical cover. Carrow and District Building Society will be the title sponsor, contributing £150,000 in return for branding on bibs, the finish arch and all publicity. About 1,200 volunteers will be needed; the council's volunteering programme will recruit and train them.

The total cost is £900,000. Entry fees of £45 per runner and sponsorship will offset part of this, but the council's cabinet has capped its net contribution at £300,000. If entries fall short of 6,000 by the end of June, the festival elements on the riverside will be reduced to protect that cap. The course must be measured and certified by an accredited course measurer before entries open. The city's safety advisory group, which includes the police, the ambulance service and the council's licensing team, must approve the event safety plan at least eight weeks before race day. Without that approval the event cannot go ahead.

The council has set sustainability targets for all major events: no single-use plastic bottles on the course (refill stations instead), 70% of event waste recycled, free bus travel for anyone showing a race number, and a published carbon footprint report within two months of the event.

The route passes two churches holding Sunday morning services and crosses the main access road to Carrowford Royal Infirmary. Residents on the route have complained on social media about being unable to drive out of their streets for five hours. The chair of the city centre traders' association says many shops lose trade when roads close, though restaurants on the riverside expect to gain. The cabinet member for leisure is highly visible in the local media and wants to start the race. Last year Paceline managed a 10k race in another city at which a runner collapsed and the medical response was criticized in an independent review.

The council's corporate risk manager has asked for the event to follow the council's risk management policy, which sets a low appetite for risks to public safety and reputation and a moderate appetite for financial risk on events. The council's internal audit team has said it will review the project at least once. The project will be managed using PRINCE2 7.

The project has four stages. Initiation will take six weeks. A planning and approvals stage will finalize the route, licences, the sponsorship contract and the volunteer plan, and open entries. A build-up stage will run marketing, train volunteers, book infrastructure and prepare the safety plan for approval. The final stage covers event week itself and six weeks afterwards for the debrief, the sponsor report, the carbon report and the economic impact study, before the event is handed to the events team to repeat.

S6.title: Brennan Mutual: Project Skyline data centre exit
S6.facts:
Brennan Mutual is a building society with 410,000 members and 38 branches in Scotland and the north of England. All its systems run in two data centres: an owned primary site near Falkirk and a leased secondary site in Leeds. The landlord of the Leeds site has said the lease, which ends in 22 months, will not be extended. Much of the hardware in both sites is near the end of its life. The board has approved a strategy to move to public cloud hosting, apart from the core banking system, which will move to the core banking vendor's own hosted service.

The chief operating officer has been given a mandate for Project Skyline: to migrate about 140 applications out of both data centres, in waves, and close them. The work includes building a secure cloud landing zone, migrating applications, moving core banking to the vendor's service, and decommissioning the old hardware. The society must notify its regulators of the material outsourcing involved, and it must show that its important member services, such as payments, online banking and branch systems, stay within the disruption limits it has set for them.

Brennan Mutual's IT department has 70 staff, but few have cloud skills. It has appointed a cloud partner, Stratoshift Ltd, under a framework contract that pays for agreed work packages at fixed day rates. Stratoshift has teams in Edinburgh and in Pune, India, so the project team will work across three locations and two time zones. The core banking vendor will move its own system under a separate contract. A previous IT project at the society, run under a single fixed-scope contract, ended in a dispute over what had been agreed.

The approved budget is £8.6 million over two years. The project must finish before the Leeds lease ends; the board wants it to finish three months before that date. The board has a very low appetite for risks that could cause outages to member-facing services or the loss of member data, and a moderate appetite for cost risk. Every migrated application must pass performance and resilience tests, have operating procedures written for the new environment and have a tested way of rolling back before it is switched over.

The business case forecasts a reduction in running costs of £1.4 million a year from year three, recovery time after a major failure cut from 24 hours to four hours, and the ability to release changes to digital services more often. The cloud provider uses renewable energy, and the society expects a 60% reduction in IT-related electricity emissions. All old hardware must be disposed of responsibly, with certificates confirming that member data has been destroyed.

About 25 people work in IT operations, many of them in data centre roles that will disappear. The society has promised retraining rather than redundancy, but several staff have said they do not trust this promise. The chief information officer wants to add a new data platform to the project. The chief risk officer insists on independent assurance of every migration wave, and the board's audit committee wants a written update every month. The society uses PRINCE2 7 for major change.

The project has five stages. Initiation will take two months. A foundations stage will build the landing zone and security controls and migrate a pilot wave of ten low-risk applications. A wave migration stage will move about 110 applications in three waves. A core banking stage will move core banking and the final applications. A decommissioning stage will remove and dispose of the hardware and close both data centres.

The executive committee has said that no migration may take place during the society's month-end processing days or its December change freeze. The chief operating officer has proposed a cost tolerance of plus or minus 7.5% for the project and wants to be told at once if any migration wave is forecast to slip by more than two weeks, because waves later in the plan depend on earlier ones.
